19946-villa-elsa-a-story-of-german-famil:
Villa Elsa calls itself a story of German family life. It opens in late summer 1913 with an American in Germany. He is a quiet college man of twenty-three, tall and lean. He has been idling on a trip without thought of adventure. He observes his surroundings without being observed, at first. Stuart Henry framed German domestic life for American readers. War was one summer away from that idyll.

American travel writers explained Germany to a curious republic. Family life made a nation legible to foreign guests. Henry's young observer drifts into the household of Villa Elsa. What he learns is the book's real plot. Read now, the calm of 1913 feels ominous. The novel preserves that last prewar summer.
20287-a-night-in-the-snow-or-a-struggle-:
A Night in the Snow, or A Struggle for Life, tells of peril in deep winter. The writer speaks of himself in a very personal manner throughout. He saw no way to give the facts without that frank approach. His duties and the country he crossed must be described firsthand.

Geography lies at the heart of this tale of snow and survival. A night exposed in such cold can kill in a few hours. The struggle of the title pits one man against storm and drift. Readers get a stark, personal record of endurance in a frozen land.
21036-my-friend-smith-a-story-of-school-:
At twelve, the teller of My Friend Smith is shipped from Brownstroke village without clear cause. Stonebridge House, an academy for backward and troublesome young gentlemen, awaits him near Cliffshire. Talbot Baines Reed opens his tale of school and city life on that exile.

Smith, the friend of the title, anchors the tale's trials and triumphs. School scrapes give way to city work, want, and hard-won rise. Reed blends his school craft with a Dickens-like city warmth here. The book ranks among his best-loved, proof that his honest, hopeful tales could grip far past the school gate.
21043-reginald-cruden-a-tale-of-city-lif:
Heat drives even Squires, the lodge keeper, to nap in his coolest nook in Reginald Cruden. Lads might take any liberty with his garden while he sleeps so sweetly. Talbot Baines Reed opens his tale of city life on that drowsy gate.

Reginald, a school lad turned city clerk, meets London's grind and glitter head-on. Want, pride, true friends, and false ones mark his climb from low rooms. Reed Dickens-like warmth for young strivers fills the book's best pages. Reginald Cruden stands among his most loved city tales, a school story grown up and set down in London's hard streets.
21045-education-and-the-higher-life:
Sacred hours when we claim the love of higher things fill Education and the Higher Life. The essayist holds that faith and hope make mortal life immortal there. A moment so filled, he writes, holds wealth that lasts through years.

Essays here urge schools to train souls, not just minds stuffed with facts. The higher life of the title means faith, taste, and moral reach. Such writing served teachers who feared mere exam craft in schools. Readers meet Victorian education thought at its most earnest, keen to wed learning to a life of depth and worth.
21137-parkhurst-boys-and-other-stories-o:
Talbot Baines Reed, the master of the school story, gathers four groups of tales in this volume. Seven Parkhurst sketches cover matches, boat races, and school events, starting with a first football match and a coveted place in the fifteen. Eleven short pieces describe types of boys, such as the Sneak.

Twelve more stories retell boys from English history, including the Princes in the Tower, Dick Whittington, and Edward the Sixth. Seven longer general stories close the book. Reed wrote for the Boy's Own Paper world, and these pieces show his range: sport, humour, history, and schoolboy character in turn.
21432-aunt-judith-the-story-of-a-loving-:
Grace Beaumont tells a schoolgirl's tale in Aunt Judith, the story of a loving life, first published in 1888. Winnifred Blake bursts into the schoolroom with news at the start. A quarrel among the girls sets the plot in motion.

At its heart stands Aunt Judith, whose talks guide Winnie and her friends. Chapters move through a Christmas party, a sailor boy, a prize essay, and gathering clouds. Choices about truth, pride, and kindness drive each turn. The tale ends in light after darkness, true to its aim. It is a warm specimen of the moral girls' story of its age.
21840-woman-her-sex-and-love-life:
Plain medical counsel for women fills this 1917 book by William J. Robinson, a New York doctor and editor of journals on urology and sexology. Robinson had written many works on sexual health, eugenics, and marriage, and edited The Critic and Guide. Here he addresses women directly on their bodies, their marriages, and their love lives. Such frankness was bold in print at the time.

The book belongs to the early fight for open sex education in America. Robinson believed ignorance, not knowledge, did the harm. He writes in a doctor's plain voice, case by case and topic by topic. Modern readers will find some views dated and others strikingly fresh. As a record of what one reforming physician dared to print in 1917, it holds its place.
22233-blazed-trail-stories-and-stories-o:
Stewart Edward White published Blazed Trail Stories and Stories of the Wild Life in 1904. White had worked in Michigan lumber camps and hunted across the continent. His title set collects tales from his popular novel The Blazed Trail and from his years in the woods. The opening story fills a lumber town's sawdust streets with Sunday crowds.

Loggers in stiff Sunday best escort their wives and sweethearts; outsiders try not to look conspicuous. White knew this world from inside and wrote it without romance or contempt. His animal stories rest on the same close watching. Few American writers of 1904 could match his record of the vanishing lumber frontier.
22295-on-prayer-and-the-contemplative-li:
On Prayer and the Contemplative Life gathers writings of St. Thomas Aquinas on the life of prayer. Its opening pages reach Aquinas's death at the abbey of Fossa Nuova. At the gates he quoted the psalm: his rest was there for ever, and there he would dwell, for he had chosen it. The great schoolman died there in 1274, worn out on a journey to a council.

The treatise that follows draws his teaching from the Summa and his commentaries. Prayer, contemplation, and the active life are weighed and ordered. Hugh Pope, the Dominican editor, made the volume for English readers. It shows the angel of the schools as a man of prayer, not only of argument.
22411-the-choice-of-life:
Georgette Leblanc wrote The Choice of Life, published in 1914. Leblanc was a French actress and writer of strong, searching temperament. Her book opens with questions she cannot shake off or answer.

Is anything definite, she asks, amid blind efforts and impulses? Since her first awakening, urges have pushed her toward other women. What had she wanted from them all that time? She stretched out her hands and searched their hearts. At times she changed the very nature of their strivings. The book pursues those questions as a spiritual autobiography. Readers meet a woman examining love, art, and freedom without flinching.
22432-parables-of-the-christ-life:
I. Lilias Trotter wrote Parables of the Christ-Life, a devotional book of plant parables. Trotter was a missionary and artist with a gift for nature imagery. Her starting text is Christ's word on being born again.

Except a man be born again, he cannot see God's kingdom. Every soul, Trotter writes, carries a possible second life. Like a flower, it holds more than its first birth shows. To souls within the Gospel's reach, a moment of receiving comes. The Life of God draws near and could be received if willing. From flowers and seeds she draws those lessons. Readers get gentle, pictured teaching on spiritual growth.
22839-jesse-cliffe:
London at dusk glows in Jesse Cliffe, a story by Mary Russell Mitford. One voice praises the prospect from Waterloo Bridge on a summer evening above all London sights. Sunset tints reflect in the Thames below. Later, lamps and boat lights blend with soft moonlight on the river.

Mitford usually writes of villages, so the city setting marks a change of air. The story carries its people between the worlds she knew, town brightness and country quiet. Talk, scenery, and character do the work that plot does in louder tales. Readers who know her through Our Village will enjoy seeing the same fond, precise eye turned on the Thames and its evening crowds.
23092-the-simple-life:
Wedding chaos crowds The Simple Life, dated 1901 in this edition. Congratulations, acceptances, and refusals pile up from attendants, alongside tradesmen's excuses. Last-minute disasters follow. A death scrambles the bridal party, and a bad cold silences the favorite singer. They will never be ready, though they thought they had foreseen everything.

Charles Wagner's plea for simpler living found millions of readers, and scenes like this wedding explain why. Modern ceremony, shopping, and display had already begun to crush the occasions they decorated. Wagner, a French pastor, writes with warmth rather than scolding. His simple life is not poverty but proportion, and the bridal panic makes his case better than any sermon.
23172-the-damned-thing-1898-from-in-the-:
Ambrose Bierce reads a dead man's diary in The Damned Thing, dated 1898, from In the Midst of Life. One reader at the inquest stands out a little, the scene notes. A man of the world, plainly, though something in his dress ties him to the wild country around him.

That dry, scientific diction is Bierce preparing his trap. A coroner's jury, a mutilated body, and a diary that blames something the eye cannot register make this his most famous horror tale. The damned thing itself stays exactly where Bierce put it, just outside human senses. Few American stories have been imitated so often, or matched so rarely. The inquest's calm procedure makes the conclusion colder than any scream.
334-episodes-in-van-bibber-s-life:
Richard Harding Davis follows Van Bibber, a cheerful young man about town, through comic episodes. Episodes in Van Bibber's Life opens behind the scenes on the first night of a comic opera, The Sultana. Anxious actors, a wardrobe woman's son, and a calm hero fill the scene.

Later episodes give Van Bibber a man servant, a hungry man fed, and a dog loved for its mistress's sake. Davis writes New York society with humor and pace. Van Bibber's politeness never breaks, even on feverish nights. The stories made Davis a favorite of magazine readers.
423-round-the-red-lamp-being-facts-and-f:
Arthur Conan Doyle gathers medical tales round the red lamp that once marked a doctor's door in this volume. Stories follow young doctors, old surgeons, and patients through births, operations, and grim wards. Doyle warns in his preface that medical life shows both heroism and bitter sorrow, and he does not soften either.

Tales include a first operation, a straggler from Waterloo, a lady's strange case, and a mummy numbered Lot 249. Some chill, some move, all show doctors as flawed, striving folk. The book stands apart from Doyle's detective work, as a grave, humane look at healing and its costs.
676-the-battle-of-life:
Charles Dickens writes a Christmas tale of love and sacrifice in this book, from the 1867 Chapman and Hall Works. The story opens on a long summer day when a fierce battle was fought in stalwart England. Its grass was stained and its stream run red, before the tale turns to two sisters and the men who love them. Years pass, and the battle's traces linger in the field.

Dickens writes with rich, lyrical prose, full of moonlight, wind, and memory. The tale asks what love costs and what it saves. It endures as a lesser-known Christmas book, where a battle's shadow gives way to a quiet, hard-won peace.
a-charmed-life:
Richard Harding Davis tells of Chesterton, a war correspondent, and the woman who loves him and fears for him. She has told him that risks taken before they met were his own affair, but now his life belongs to her too. When war comes and the Maine has sunk in Havana harbor, he goes anyway.

Word reaches her that he has been shot, and the tale turns on what she believes and what is true. Davis builds the story on the strange luck that has guarded Chesterton through past wars, watched from inside a British square and among frightened camels. The ending tests whether his charm can hold one more time.
a-daughter-of-fife:
Amelia E. Barr opens on the shore of a little land-locked haven in the East Neuk of Fife, where gulls bring tidings of the sea to the fishing hamlet of Pittenloch. Some cottages stand on the sands, others grouped above. Her contents begin with The Beached Boat and The Unknown Guest, then The Campbells of Meriton.

Maggie, the daughter of Fife, and Angus carry the love story through parting, a broken sixpence, Maggie's flight, a journey to the Hebrides, and a broken tryst. Barr, born in England and long resident in America, wrote many such tales of the old country. Her Scots fisherfolk speak in dialect, pray hard, and hold their honor higher than comfort.
a-day-in-old-athens-a-picture-of-athenia:
William Stearns Davis wrote A Day in Old Athens to show a visitor the city in the year 360 B.C. Davis, professor of ancient history at the University of Minnesota, explains his choice in the preface. Athens then stood architecturally almost perfect, her democracy vigorous. Few signs yet showed the decadence that followed Macedon's triumph.

The tour begins with Attica's mountains, sunlight, and sterile soil. Morning crowds stream through the gates into streets of simple house fronts. The agora, the marketplace, fills with booths, fish vendors, and leisured talkers. Chapters enter an Athenian house and follow a gentleman home. Davis drew on Greek writers first and modern scholarship second. His picture suits readers with school Greek history who want daily life, not battles: barbers, flowers, and dinner talk.
a-mummer-s-wife:
George Moore wrote A Mummer's Wife as a naturalistic novel of the stage, and the hosted edition carries his dedication to the critic Robert Ross. Its heroine is Kate Ede, a young woman behind a draper's counter in the Potteries. Starved of colour and romance in a dull marriage to an ailing shopkeeper and a duller round of work.

A travelling theatre company brings the actor Dick Lennox into her life, and she runs off into the mummer's world of lodgings, rehearsals, and one-night towns. Moore follows the price without melodrama: drink, decline, and the slow loss of the very glamour she fled to find. The novel made his name in England as a follower of Zola's method, honest about lives that novels then usually prettied up.
a-rogue-s-life:
Wilkie Collins tells the confessions of Frank Softly, a cheerful rogue who narrates his own scrapes with pride. Collins's opening words explain that the tale first ran in Dickens's Household Words more than twenty years before this edition, and that he meant to enlarge its Australian ending but never did. The story stands as he left it.

Frank drifts from a respectable family into forgery's edge, quack medicine, picture dealing, and a voyage to Australia as a transported man. Each scheme begins in hope and ends in flight or exposure. Collins keeps the tone light and the pace quick, and Frank's shameless good humor carries the reader along.
a-start-in-life:
Honoré de Balzac follows young Oscar Husson, a Paris clerk's son with fine dreams and little sense, in Katharine Prescott Wormeley's translation. The opening chapter looks back at the old stage-coaches, called coucous, that still ran around Paris in the 1820s. On one such coach ride, Oscar's boasting sets his troubles in motion.

Eleven chapters trace his showing off before a great lord's steward, the harm his loose tongue does, and his family's pain and sacrifice. A mother's trials, a posting abroad, and one last blunder fill the later chapters. Balzac treats Oscar's fall and slow repair as a lesson in how a career truly begins.
allan-s-wife:
H. Rider Haggard dedicates this Allan Quatermain tale to the friend whose native name, Macumazahn, he borrowed for his hero. The contents run from Quatermain's early days through a fire-fight, a Zulu impi, and the end of a laager, to the chapter simply titled Stella. She is the wife of the title, met in the wild country.

Later chapters bring the baboon-woman Hendrika, marble kraals, a plot of evil, and loss, closing fifteen years after. Quatermain tells the story himself, looking back on the great love and grief of his life between hunts and wars. Haggard mixes adventure with an elegy, and the book deepens the hunter his readers already knew from King Solomon's Mines.
american-literary-centers-from-literatur:
William Dean Howells argues a cheerful paradox: America has much literature but no literary centre. Where there is so much smoke, he writes, there must be a fireplace — yet America has a dozen fireplaces, which is as bad as none. The essay comes from his volume Literature and Life.

He looks back at papers he wrote years before and takes the question up again, prompted by a query from England. Boston's old reign, New York's publishing power, and the rising West all come under review. Howells, who had stood at the center of American letters himself, writes with inside knowledge and gentle irony about how a scattered country makes its books.
an-outback-marriage-a-story-of-australia:
An Outback Marriage, a story of Australian life by Andrew Barton Paterson, better known as Banjo Paterson of The Man from Snowy River, opens in a Sydney club. Paterson's contents move from a dinner for five into push society, the city's larrikin underworld, then out to the old station. The coming of the heiress changes the board, and a coach accident brings Mr Blake's relations into play at the homestead.

Blake breaks his engagement, rivals multiply, and Red Mick appears with his sheep dogs. A walk in the moonlight and a proposal lead down the road to No Man's Land, where the lost Considine must be searched for twice and saved from a buffalo camp. A real certificate, a legal battle, and races with a win close the account. Paterson writes the bush he rode as a solicitor and journalist.
auriol-or-the-elixir-of-life: Ainsworth's Auriol seeks the elixir of life. The Rosicrucian tale spans centuries. The Gothic romance endures. Its contents inform the historical record. The book preserves that novel. Readers can find it here. The volume endures.
cardano-book-of-my-life:
Girolamo Cardano, a Milanese physician and mathematician, wrote The Book of My Life in the 1570s, near his death. Jean Stoner's 1930 English translation is the version here. Cardano was famous, quarrelsome, and unlucky, and he hides none of it.

He catalogues his diseases, his dreams, his gambling, and his feuds with rivals and sons. One son was executed; the grief haunts the book. Cardano also helped found algebra and wrote early work on chance. Few Renaissance lives are told with such startling candor, down to his teeth, his diet, and his horoscope. Stoner's version keeps his odd, list-loving voice clear for modern readers.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abbey-of-flor:
The Catholic Encyclopedia entry on Floreffe describes a Norbertine abbey pleasantly set on the Sambre, seven miles south-west of Namur, founded by Count Godfrey of Namur together with Ermensendis, his wife. When St. Norbert returned from Cologne with relics for Prémontré, the count and countess met him at Namur and begged him to found a house at Floreffe.

Their charter of November 1121, giving a church and house to Norbert's order, makes Floreffe chronologically the order's second abbey. Norbert laid the church's foundations, calling it Salve, and the abbey took the sweet name Flos Mariae, Flower of Mary. The chronicles record a Mass at which Norbert saw a drop of blood issue from the Host to the paten.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alife:
Alife is a diocese of twelve communes in Caserta province, in Benevento's archbishopric, Italy. A Bishop of Alife first appears among those signing at the Roman Synod of 499, under Pope Symmachus. He signs Clarus episcopus Ecclesiae Allifanae subscripsi, as the Monumenta Germaniae Historica records. Twelve communes make up a compact Caserta diocese in Italy.

The diocese holds 17 parishes, 60 priests, and 23,890 inhabitants in all today. Its recorded history thus opens with one synod signature back in 499. The signature stands as the diocese's first certain trace, with any earlier origins still unrecorded.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-brethren-of-t:
The Brethren of the Common Life, founded by Geert Groote of Deventer, renewed Dutch faith through preaching, schools, and books without monastic vows. Born in 1340 to rich burgher stock, Groote studied at Cologne, the Sorbonne, and Prague, held canonries at Utrecht and Aachen, and turned to mysticism under Ruysbroek's influence. Recovering from illness in 1373, he gave his goods to the Arnheim Carthusians and lived seven years alone.

Going out to preach repentance and divine love, he drew thousands and gathered a band of fellow workers, the first Brethren. Opponents cried heresy in vain against a man zealous for pure faith and morals. After his death in 1384, Florence Radewyns founded Windesheim in 1386 as the association's center. Members took no vows, sought no alms, worked for bread, and poured their houses into literature, teaching, and preaching.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-contemplative:
Edmund Gurdon's entry defines contemplative life as a life ordered toward contemplation, excluding other preoccupations and intents. Seeking to know and love God more binds every Christian, so in a wide sense Christian and contemplative lives are synonymous. Fulfillment admits degrees. Others blend contemplation with active ministry, care of souls, which charity can render compatible with inner life.

Contemplation means the soul's loving gaze on Divine truth already known and grasped by intellect. Love for Divine things drives the contemplative, and love's increase forms its purpose and firstfruits. The act, imperfect as it must be, ranks among the most sublime human acts, honoring God and benefiting souls. Religious life, essentially self-denial, counters self-seeking through contemplative orders' rules. Contemplatives' great function remains God's worship, and love for God breeds love for fellow-men, the two growing apace.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-edward-metcal:
Edward Metcalfe was a Yorkshire Benedictine remembered as a martyr of charity, born in 1792 and dead at Leeds in 1847. He entered Ampleforth in 1811, was ordained five years later, and soon stood out as a linguist. After mission work at Kilvington he helped found a monastery at Prior Park near Bath. In 1830 Rome let the group answer to the vicar apostolic. A misunderstanding later left them secularised.

As chaplain to Sir Edward Mostyn at Talacre he learned Welsh so he could serve Welsh people, then served at Newport and Bristol. With readmission to the Benedictines nearly settled in 1847, he heard of fever at Leeds, offered himself to the bishop there, and hastened to the stricken town. He soon caught the fever himself and died, leaving Welsh versions of Challoner's devotional works.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-konrad-der-pf: A 1913 entry on Konrad the Priest — the Roland singer. Arthur F.J. Remy honors his famous Rolandslied. His verse sang the Roncevaux fight. Germany loved the martial muse. The twelfth century knew his name. His 1170 death is famed. His 1170 Roland is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-life: A 1913 entry on Life — the vital principle. Michael Maher unfolds its scholastic lore. The soul informs the living frame. The schools prized the seemly bounds. The philosophers weigh its kinds. Its 1907 study is famed. Its scholastic form is famed. Its 1907 vital principle is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-religious-lif: The religious life is the state of the evangelical counsels. This long entry treats its nature, its vows, and its excellence. The following of Christ in perfection: its three counsels free the heart from earthly cares and chains and noise.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-stephen-goffe: Stephen Goffe was the English royalist. This entry traces his Charles, his Paris, and his fame. The divine of the exiled court: his staunch loyalty crowned Paris in the 1640s' exile in the city of the Seine in old France.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-teneriffe: Teneriffe is the diocese of the Canaries. This entry traces its Laguna, its bishops, and its churches. The bishopric of the Atlantic isles: its new see crowned La Laguna in the 1810s' island in the ocean of the far west.
certain-diversities-of-american-life:
Charles Dudley Warner surveys his country's recent changes in this essay on American life, and he opens with sport. Within a generation the trotting record has fallen, and baseball has grown from a boys' pastime into a national industry. Newspapers, he notes, give more columns to the game than to any other subject in the American mind.

From the pitcher, paid more than a college president, Warner turns to the colleges themselves. Technical education advances, the elective system spreads, and boat crews advertise a university better than scholars do. The standard of a fortune has shifted from competence to millions in the same years. His theme is diversity: a country getting richer, faster, and more practical, and not stopping to ask at what cost.
chaucer-s-official-life:
James Root Hulbert's Chaucer's Official Life reconstructs the public career of Geoffrey Chaucer from the documents of the English Public Record Office. Rather than retelling the poems, Hulbert follows Chaucer through the offices and duties that filled his working life.

The study leans on Close Rolls, the Life Records of Chaucer published by the Chaucer Society, and other calendars of state papers, preferring printed calendars where readers can check them. Hulbert warns frankly that copying so many references invites small errors, and he thanks the keepers at the British Museum and the Record Office who opened manuscripts to him. Scholars of Chaucer and of medieval administration will value its careful, document-by-document method.
confessions-of-a-summer-colonist-from-li:
William Dean Howells wrote Confessions of a Summer Colonist as a reflective essay drawn from Literature and Life, his collection of studies. Howells spends three months in a small summer settlement on the Down East coast of Maine. The season is ending as he writes. He already feels homesick for a place he has not yet left.

Howells describes the colony's fragile cottages, its seven-o'clock suppers, and its proud informality. Men refuse to dress for supper while ladies supply the ceremony. He sees the settlement caught between rough early days and coming vulgar luxury. Small social habits reveal, for him, something deeply American. Readers get a gentle, observant portrait of summer-colony life before it vanished, written by a novelist who noticed manners the way other men notice weather.
diary-of-samuel-pepys-volume-01-preface-:
Volume 01 of this edition of Samuel Pepys's Diary holds no diary at all: it is the Preface and Life, Henry B. Wheatley's front matter for the first complete printing. The preface tells the Diary's own strange history. Pepys wrote it in shorthand in six volumes now kept at Magdalene College, Cambridge, his old college. Lord Braybrooke's edition of 1825 printed barely half the manuscript; Mynors Bright later added a third more, and Wheatley's edition at last gives the whole.

A Life of Pepys follows, from his Brampton childhood and St. Paul's schooling to the Navy Office and the Royal Society presidency. The shorthand, the cipher passages, and the famous library Pepys left to Magdalene are all explained. Readers starting the Diary should start here. Wheatley's apparatus turns a decoded notebook into the best-known portrait of Restoration London. It also explains why the world waited two centuries to read it entire.
diddie-dumps-and-tot-or-plantation-child:
Louise Clarke Pyrnelle's Diddie, Dumps, and Tot, first copyrighted in 1882, preserves the plantation childhood she remembered. Her preface states the aim: to keep alive the old stories, legends, games, and hymns of the enslaved people. Their tellers, the mammies and uncles of her nursery, were passing away. She disclaims any defence of slavery, she writes, telling only of pleasant relations.

Three little white sisters, Diddie, Dumps, and Tot, hear Mammy's stories and Uncle Bob's Sunday school. Christmas on the old plantation and the Fourth of July frame the year. Black storytellers explain how the woodpecker's head and the robin's breast came to be red. Pyrnelle prints dialect tales as she heard them in Alabama. Modern readers will find both genuine folklore and a slaveholder's daughter's softened memory, bound in one historically telling volume.
doe-osti-2589185-the-effect-of-heat-trea: Heat-treated 3D-printed steel got its defect study, and this DOE report tracks LPBF 316H evolution. The pages detail the metallurgy. The materials scientists get their data. The steel was 316H stainless. The evolution was defect. The scientists got data.
doe-osti-3005046-comport-rigorous-testin: ComPort got its rigorous testing, and this DOE UW final safeguards software porting. The pages detail the method findings. The software folks get their closeout. The porting was software. The closeout was software. The report was UW. The methods were rigorous.
doe-osti-3016268-colorado-pueblo-regiona: Pueblo got DAC-hubbed, and this DOE final studies phase 0a feasibility. The pages detail the technical findings. The climate folks get their closeout. The city was Pueblo. The closeout was climate. The feasibility was phase. The report was technical.
doe-osti-3020599-glass-formulation-devel: Phosphate HLW got glass-formulated, and this DOE text develops Al, Fe, Na glass. The pages detail the findings. The nuclear folks get their data. The HLW was phosphate. The data were nuclear. The Na was Fe. The phosphate was HLW.
doe-osti-3399560-evaluating-polymer-prop: Catching CO2 from smokestacks needs materials that grab the gas and let go on command. Stiles and Ye evaluate how different additives change polymer properties for carbon capture and other uses. The right additive recipe could make capture membranes cheaper and tougher.
eclectic-school-readings-stories-from-li:
Orison Swett Marden compiled Eclectic School Readings: Stories from Life as a book for young people. Marden, founder of Success magazine, states his aim in the preface. To make a life matters more than to make a living. Brief stories of great lives show poor boys rising by character.

The Mill Boy of the Slashes, Andrew Jackson the boy who never would give up, opens the examples. Farragut, Gladstone, and Gambetta appear beside the Greek slave who won the olive crown. Sir Humphry Davy's greatest discovery, Michael Faraday, gets a chapter of his own. Franklin teaches the value of time, and Canova triumphs over poverty. Marden thanks Margaret Connolly for help in preparing the volume. It is schoolroom self-help, earnest and anecdotal, built to be read aloud.
episodes-in-van-bibber-s-life:
Richard Harding Davis built these tales around Courtlandt Van Bibber. Davis was the dashing war reporter and story writer of the 1890s. Van Bibber is a young New York man of wealth and perfect manners. He moves through clubs, theaters, roof gardens, and country houses. He is forever rescuing friends from scrapes. A chorus girl must be saved from a bad marriage. A prizefighter must be hidden. A duel must be stopped before breakfast.

Davis tells each episode with speed and polish. Van Bibber, for all his polish, keeps a kind heart and a quick hand. The stories fixed the image of the American gentleman hero for their age. Davis lived much the same glamorous life himself. He became a model for a generation of reporters.
far-away-and-long-ago-a-history-of-my-ea:
Far Away and Long Ago, by W H Hudson, recalls his childhood on the Argentine pampas. Hudson's contents start with earliest memories. They name the house where he was born in Argentina. They name a singular ombu tree and the open pampas plain. A ghost said to haunt the plain appears. So does an old sheep dog, his playmate. A first riding lesson among the cattle at evening closes the list.

Later chapters move the family to a new home. A schoolmaster, Mr Trigg, impersonates an old woman and reads Dickens aloud. A whole chapter goes to the death of Caesar, the old dog. It is Hudson's first encounter with mortality, and his mother's comfort. Hudson writes natural history as autobiography. Birds, horses, and plains weather form the boy as much as people do.
finger-posts-on-the-way-of-life:
T. S. Arthur's Finger Posts on the Way of Life, published in 1853, offers tales as road signs for travellers. Arthur explains the quaint title in his preface. Life's path is new and strange to each of us, often rough and dark. His little book points the wary walker in the right direction.

Shadows from a Clouded Brow opens the collection with the Abercrombies' touchy marriage. Other pieces ask Will It Pay and show how to destroy a good business. The Little Bound-Boy, The Lay Preacher, and Marrying Well give the set its range. Arthur insists that natural life exists for the sake of spiritual life. His finger-posts point through the world toward heaven. The tales are brief, earnest, and aimed at readers who wanted fiction with a conscience in every scene.
for-the-term-of-his-natural-life:
Marcus Clarke wrote For the Term of His Natural Life, the great Australian convict novel, drawing on records of the transportation system. Clarke's dedication explains his aim plainly. Earlier fiction, he says, showed convicts only before or after their punishment. He wanted to show the punishment itself. His hero is Rufus Dawes, a transported man caught in that system.

Dawes endures the penal stations of Macquarie Harbour, Port Arthur, and Norfolk Island. Chaplain James North and officer Maurice Frere frame his suffering from opposite sides. A ship mutiny, escapes, and slow spiritual breaking fill the long narrative. Clarke insists his horrors rest on events that actually happened. Readers get a fierce indictment of a punishment regime, carried by a story of endurance, guilt, and unlikely redemption.
gaut-gurley-or-the-trappers-of-umbagog-a:
Daniel P. Thompson's Gaut Gurley, or The Trappers of Umbagog, is a tale of border life between Vermont, New Hampshire and Canada. The story contrasts town and country in relation to vice and crime, opening with a display party meant to avoid bankruptcy.

A country merchant climbs toward becoming a solid man of Boston, lured into running goods across the Canadian line while trade was banned, with Gaut Gurley's desperate help. Gambling, failure and family distress follow, as the merchant's brother refuses aid and the household shares his degradation. Thompson writes a moral frontier tale, and readers of early American fiction will find its smuggling scenes and trappers vivid.
geological-contemporaneity-and-persisten:
Thomas Henry Huxley gave this address to the anniversary meeting of the Geological Society as a stocktaking of palaeontology, the study of fossil remains. He borrows the merchant's habit of taking stock: after speculation, face the facts and count the solid gold of truth. His first entry is the flood of new species fossils had added to the catalogues of botany and zoology, near forty thousand of them.

Two problems govern the address. The first is contemporaneity: whether rock layers in distant places can truly be called the same age. The second is the persistent types of life named in his title, forms that run unchanged through great thicknesses of rock. Such survivors trouble any simple story of steady development, and Huxley weighs what they do and do not disprove.
harry-heathcote-of-gangoil-a-tale-of-aus:
Harry Heathcote of Gangoil, a tale of Australian bush life by Anthony Trollope, follows a young sheep farmer at odds with his neighbors. Trollope sets the opening a fortnight before Christmas in 1871, high summer in Australia. Harry, twenty four years old and married, comes home to dinner at eight with his wife and her sister in the house, and tension already in the air.

Twelve chapters move from the station at Gangoil to a night ride, Medlicot's mill, and Harry's appeal for fair treatment. The Brownbies of Boolabong stand as his enemies, and headings promise a bush fight before Harry returns in triumph. Sergeant Forrest and a conclusion settle the feud. Trollope, who knew Australia from travel, writes about fences, fires, and pride of independence in a settler world where a man's name travels faster than any horse.
he-fell-in-love-with-his-wife:
Edward Payson Roe built He Fell in Love with His Wife around James Holcroft, a widowed farmer who needs a housekeeper and dreads a wife. The matchmaking widow Mrs. Mumpson negotiates, schemes, and fails him, chapter by chapter. Holcroft's business solution is a marriage of convenience with Alida, a homeless woman who needs shelter more than romance, described in the contents as not wife, but waif.

Farm routine, village gossip, and a charivari, the noisy mock serenade of newlyweds, fill the middle chapters. Slowly the arrangement warms into regard, then love, as Alida's work and character transform the farm. Roe, a minister turned novelist, wrote domestic stories for a huge popular audience, and this was among his best loved.
heartsease-or-the-brother-s-wife: Heartsease, or The Brother's Wife, by Charlotte Yonge. The family tale. This book preserves that Victorian novel. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it.
henson-life:
Josiah Henson published his Life in 1849, telling how he rose from slavery in Maryland to freedom in Canada. Henson was the trusted driver of his owner's plantation, yet still cheated of a promised freedom. His story reached a huge audience.

He recounts carrying his master's son to Kentucky, his preaching, and his daring escape with his wife and children. In Canada he helped found Dawn, a settlement where refugee families could farm and learn. Harriet Beecher Stowe drew on Henson's life for Uncle Tom. His narrative blends faith, shrewdness, and quiet pride. Dawn's school and mill showed what free Black settlers could build.
how-to-live-a-holy-life:
Charles Ebert Orr's How to Live a Holy Life is a devotional manual on the Christian life. Orr opens with devotional reading itself, arguing that you can nearly judge a person by the books he reads, since the nature of one's books is usually the nature of one's thoughts.

Readers who love spiritual books prosper in the Lord, Orr says, while those without a relish for them labour at great disadvantage. The most spiritual men of all ages, he adds, loved spiritual reading strongly. The book then guides the reader through prayer, purity and daily conduct toward holiness. Believers seeking plain, earnest devotional counsel will find Orr direct and encouraging.
jewel-a-chapter-in-her-life:
Clara Louise Burnham published this novel with Grosset and Dunlap in 1903, and it became her best-known story. The chapter list opens with Jewel's arrival at her grandfather's house, where the little girl is to stay while her parents travel. Mr. Evringham is stern, his housekeeper colder still, and the coachman 'Zekiel is the first friendly face the child meets.

Jewel carries into that gloomy house the Christian Science faith her mother taught her, and Burnham shows it working person by person. Chapters on her first lesson, a Wednesday evening meeting, and the doctor's visits mark the household's slow softening. A sick horse, a selfish cousin, and a grandfather's pride all yield to the child's steady practice of love. It is a domestic novel written as gentle persuasion for its faith.
jim-waring-of-sonora-town-or-tang-of-lif:
Jim Waring of Sonora-Town, or Tang of Life, is a Western tale by Henry Herbert Knibbs. The sample opens in verse, not prose, with Waring riding down from Salvador. August 1918 is the date on its title pages, and E. Boyd Smith drew the pictures. Knibbs was already known for Overland Red.

In the poem, heat swims over the desert as Waring rides, singing low to his pony's steps. His eye keeps drifting over the mesquite, sifting every crawling shadow. In a hollow an outlaw waits, hoping to shoot him in the back as he turns. Waring spots a shiny ring gleaming where no ring should grow. The verse sets up a gunman hero whose calm hides constant watchfulness.
john-henry-smith-a-humorous-romance-of-o:
John Henry Smith is a humorous romance of outdoor life by Frederick Upham Adams, published in 1905. Adams also wrote John Burt and The Kidnapped Millionaires. The book pretends to be Smith's own diary, edited at his request. In a note to the reader, the editor admits he changed only the characters' names.

He kept Smith's people exactly as Smith drew them, faults and all. He also reprints some of Smith's own sketches. The editor teases that Smith has literary, artistic, and athletic gifts, plus rare good fortune. A. B. Frost supplied the pictures. The result is a comic sporting tale told as a gentleman's diary of outdoor pleasures.
justice-in-the-by-ways-a-tale-of-life:
Justice in the By-Ways, a Tale of Life, is a novel by F. Colburn Adams, author of Our World. It was published at New York and London in 1856. An epigraph warns that corruption of principles ruins a people more surely than rebellion or invasion. The contents open aboard the brig Standfast, with Tom Swiggs's seventh introduction.

Madame Flamingo and her respectable house, Mr. Snivel the accommodation man, and George Mullholland enter early. Anna Bonard's history gets a gleam of light in a later chapter. Mr. Absalom McArthur makes a discovery, and Tom Swiggs gains his liberty. Adams weaves low-life scenes and respectable hypocrisy into a tale about how justice actually works in the by-ways.
kokoro-hints-and-echoes-of-japanese-inne:
Lafcadio Hearn wrote Kokoro at Kobe in September 1895. He explains that kokoro means heart, and also mind, spirit, courage, and inner meaning. The papers here treat the inner life of Japan, not its outer life.

Essays visit a railway station, a street singer, and a nun's temple. Others treat karma, ancestor worship, and life after a war. Hearn watches small scenes closely and draws large meanings from them. Readers come to this book for a gentle, thoughtful portrait of Japanese feeling. Hearn lived in Japan and wrote for Western readers abroad. His respect for the inner life he describes shapes every essay.
last-days-in-a-dutch-hotel-from-literatu:
William Dean Howells wrote Last Days in a Dutch Hotel in 1897. It forms part of his book Literature and Life. The piece recalls a stay at Scheveningen in mid-September.

A hotel porter at The Hague warned them they would be cold. He was right: wind blew for a whole week. About a hundred guests rustled through the chilly halls like autumn leaves. Howells turns that thin, late season crowd into gentle comedy. His travel sketch shows a master of realism at his most relaxed. Small discomforts fill the sketch rather than grand sights. Howells finds character in porters, guests, and bad weather alike.
little-citizens-the-humours-of-school-li:
Myra Kelly gathers funny, tender stories of school life here. W. D. Stevens illustrated the volume for its readers. A Little Matter of Real Estate opens the contents. The Uses of Adversity and Love Among the Blackboards follow.

Morris and the Honourable Tim play out classroom diplomacy. H.R.H. The Prince of Hester Street promises neighborhood royalty. A Passport to Paradise and The Touch of Nature close the list. Kelly taught immigrant children on New York's Lower East Side. Isidore Belchatosky appears among the illustrated classroom characters. Teacher, I tells you 'scuse, one caption quotes a pupil.
livermore-story-of-my-life:
Mary Livermore published The Story of My Life in 1897, subtitled the sunshine and shadow of seventy years. Livermore had been a Civil War nurse and a lead organizer of the Sanitary Commission's Chicago work. After the war she became a famed suffrage speaker.

She tells of her New England girlhood, teaching in the South, and the Chicago fairs that raised funds for soldiers. Her lectures for women's votes fill the later chapters, along with tales of the lecture circuit. Livermore writes warmly of friends like Julia Ward Howe. The book tracks one woman's path from nurse to national voice.
lord-tony-s-wife:
Lord Tony's Wife, published in 1917, is one of Baroness Orczy's Scarlet Pimpernel novels. It is set in France as revolution gathers force. The prologue opens in Nantes in 1789, in a low tavern room. There a young man named Pierre listens to talk of the Rights of Man, and hate burns in him.

From that seed of hate the story grows toward the Terror that follows. Lord Tony, a friend of the Scarlet Pimpernel, has a French wife caught in the danger. Orczy mixes romance, disguise, and rescue in her well-known style. The novel shows how old wrongs fed the fury of the Revolution. It also tests love and loyalty when a whole country turns violent.
making-the-most-of-life:
Making the Most of Life is a book of earnest chapters by J. R. Miller. Thomas Y. Crowell published it at New York, copyrighted 1891. Miller also wrote Silent Times and Building of Character. An introduction quotes Alexander on Aristotle, who taught him how to live.

Life, Miller says, is God's most sacred trust, to be accounted for. His chapters press duty, thoughtfulness, and self-renunciation. He leaves small space for play, and says plainly that he means to. The aim is to stir readers toward worthy, careful living. Miller was a Presbyterian pastor beloved for such counsel. His books guided millions of Victorian Christians at home.
man-and-wife:
Man and Wife is a novel by Wilkie Collins, dated 1870. A prologue called 'The Irish Marriage' stands before the story proper. The tale then unfolds in scenes, opening at a summer-house. An inn supplies the second scene of the opening part.

Collins builds his plot on the traps inside marriage law. A woman may find herself bound — or not bound — by a quirk. Anne and Blanche, school friends, stand at the story's heart. One of them falls into the power of a scoundrel. Collins turns legal detail into high suspense. He also attacks the laws that made such traps possible. The novel is sensation fiction with a reformer's purpose.
marguerite-verne-or-scenes-from-canadian:
Marguerite Verne offers scenes from Canadian life by Rebecca Agatha Armour. It opens on New Year's Eve in the city of St. John. That 'queenly little city' sits on her rocky throne over the bay. The narrator will not apologize for loving New Brunswick.

Pride in being a British subject warms the book's first pages. Through Marguerite's story, Armour paints her young Dominion's society. Balls, visits, and churchgoing fill the colonial city's seasons. Love and duty test her heroine among her neighbors. The novel is among the early works of Canadian fiction by a woman. Its local color now reads as precious history.
married-life:
Married Life, or The True Romance, is a novel by May Edginton. Small, Maynard published it at Boston in 1920. Edginton dedicated it in admiration to a completely successful husband. Its chapters read like the stations of a marriage itself.

Anticipation comes first, then Irrevocable, then Beautiful Dreams. Housekeeping and Discipline follow, as they must in life. Disillusion arrives, then Baby, then Problems and Recrimination. 'The Banged Door' names the crisis every reader dreads. Edginton asks what romance survives the daily round. Her answer is honest about quarrels, money, and making up. The book speaks plainly to couples of its day.
mary-olivier-a-life:
May Sinclair published Mary Olivier: A Life in 1919. Five books divide one woman's span into clear stages. They run from birth in 1865 through middle age in 1910.

The first book covers the years 1865 to 1869, in a cot. Young Mary watches the folds of a bed curtain in the dark. Shapes in the cloth seem to move, grin, and hide from her gaze. Sinclair tells a whole life from inside one sharp, watching mind. Childhood, youth, and the years to 1900 fill the books between. The span lets readers watch one self form across a full life.
meadow-grass-tales-of-new-england-life:
Alice Brown published Meadow Grass: Tales of New England Life in 1895. Twelve tales fill the book, each set in her home region. Number Five leads, and Farmer Eli's Vacation comes second.

Told in the Poorhouse and Heman's Ma bring plain folk to the fore. Joint Owners in Spain adds a touch of farce to the set. Nancy Boyd's Last Sermon and Strollers in Tiverton close the list. Brown writes of Tiverton born folk, loyal to woods, field, and sea. After All and At Sudleigh Fair widen the set's small town world. Brown's folk speak in local turns that fix place and class.
memoirs-of-my-dead-life:
George Moore's Memoirs of My Dead Life opens with an Apologia. That Latin head means a defense of his own writings. A note from the publisher tells why that defense was written.

Spring in London and Flowering Normandy lead the chapter list. A Waitress, The End of Marie Pellegrin, and La Butte follow. Spent Loves, Ninon's Table d'Hote, and The Lovers of Orelay come next. Sunday Evening in London and a last head, Resurgam, close the book. In the Luxembourg Gardens and A Remembrance add softer notes. Moore looks back on loves, towns, and tables long past.
nasa-tm-19680015146-determination-of-con:
Ronald G. Huff of Lewis Research Center presents a new way to measure heat transfer at insulated walls in this 1968 report. Engineers need convective heat transfer coefficients to predict how hot surfaces get in flowing fluids. Huff's method watches how an insulated wall responds when fluid temperature swings in a steady wave pattern.

From that response, the coefficient can be calculated directly. An exact solution accounts for heat conduction and for where the wall temperature is sensed. Charts in the report support the method for one-dimensional heat flow cases. The approach lets engineers measure heat transfer on walls that stay adiabatic, or nearly heat-proof, during tests.
nick-of-the-woods-or-adventures-of-prair:
Robert Montgomery Bird, a doctor, wrote Nick of the Woods, or Adventures of Prairie Life. His preface picks a fight with the frontier tales before his. Chateaubriand and Cooper, he says, had thrown a poetic glow over the Indian character. Readers had come to see red men as nature's nobles.

Bird calls such figures beautiful unrealities, like Atala and Uncas. No race in an uncivil state, he argues, matches that tender, refined image. Travellers and lawmakers, he says, find nothing like it among the tribes they know. His own tale aims at a harder picture of prairie life. Modern readers will judge his counter claim with care.
notes-by-the-way-in-a-sailor-s-life:
Captain Arthur E. Knights wrote his Notes by the Way in a Sailor's Life as letters, at a friend's urging. In Hongkong in 1898, he explains, China Mail editor Murray Bain asked why he never sent a letter. Those letters became the notes. Friends then pressed him to print them as a pamphlet for private sharing.

Contents list a quick passage and a record long passage, then a voyage of misfortune. The beginning of the German navy and an incident in Hongkong harbour follow. A Brazilian slaver, a singular meeting, and a good record in life saving appear. One piece asks if fatality attaches to men or things. Knights begs sailor's pardon for his writing.
old-creole-days-a-story-of-creole-life:
George Washington Cable wrote these stories of Creole New Orleans. This edition was printed in 1907. The contents list seven tales, starting with Madame Delphine. Other tales name Jean-ah Poquelin and 'Tite Poulette. Cable sets the scenes in old streets near Canal Street.

The opening tale walks readers into the quiet Royal Street. Old houses, flower women, and decayed shops set the mood. Cable writes about a proud, fading Creole world. Love, honor, and family secrets drive the stories. The book remains a key portrait of old New Orleans. Cable's ear for speech and place gives each tale a strong local flavor.
one-woman-s-life:
Robert Herrick published this novel with Macmillan in 1913. He had written Together and The Healer before it. Part one is called The West Side. Its chapters follow a young woman named Milly. Milly settles in a new home and goes to church.

Milly completes her education and experiments with the world. She runs a campaign and wins achievements in part one. Part two is called Getting Married, by its heading. Herrick traces one woman's growth, choices, and ambitions. The contents promise a full life story in stages. It suits readers of realistic American novels.
paris-with-pen-and-pencil-its-people-and:
David W. Bartlett's Paris: With Pen and Pencil promises the city's people and literature. Its life and business follow in the subtitle. Bartlett had already written What I Saw in London. Lives of Lady Jane Grey and Joan of Arc were also his. His preface explains the book's two Parises. He visited twice, under two regimes.

The first visit came when Louis Napoleon was president of the Republic. The second came when Napoleon the Third was emperor. Bartlett sketched people and places as he saw them at both periods. He warns readers to bear the double date in mind. The book is no handbook, he insists. He describes only what came under his own notice. Sketches of literary men fill the space other writers give to streets.
podcast-joerogan-BQmV3rU8ifE:
Author Lawrence Wright joins Joe Rogan to talk Scientology and Tom Cruise in a segment drawn from his Going Clear work. Wright wrote the famed book and film on the church. His reporting took him deep into a closed faith.

Wright tells how the church holds its stars and why Cruise sits at its core. He shares what ex-members told him of life inside and the price of flight. Rogan asks what most shocks a man who has seen it all. Listeners get the short form of a landmark probe. The library holds the segment as an archive record.
podcast-joerogan-DgSLkakMDfE:
Dr. Rhonda Patrick joins the Joe Rogan Experience for episode 502, an early entry in her long run as the show's nutrition guide. Patrick is a biomedical researcher who turns lab findings into plain advice. Her visits are among the most note-taking-heavy hours the show produces.

She walks Rogan through the science of food, vitamins, and the genes that change how bodies respond to both. Rogan asks what to eat, what to skip, and what the studies really prove. Listeners get a dense but clear briefing on eating for long-term health, from a researcher who cites her sources as she goes.
podcast-tuckercarlson-M58G-zmqifE:
Hunter Biden, the president's son, sits for a long interview with Tucker Carlson in this episode. Hunter's life of addiction, business deals, and a famous abandoned laptop made him a central figure in his father's scandals. A sit-down with his father's fiercest critic is a stunning pairing.

Hunter speaks at length about the laptop, the drugs, and the family business in his own words. Carlson asks the questions his audience most wants put to the man himself. The tone stays calmer than the subject usually allows. Political and stunned viewers get the president's son unscripted, facing his toughest interviewer.
podcast-tuckercarlson-bd9Uftz1hfE:
Tucker Carlson gives a full speech in Melbourne, Australia, and this episode holds the whole talk. The title calls it a warning to Australians. He speaks to a live crowd on a tour far from home.

Carlson warns the crowd about free speech laws, Covid-era rules, and what he sees as the West in decline. He urges Australians to guard their rights before they slip away. The crowd hears the same case he makes at home, tuned to their own fights. Listeners get the full speech in one file, start to end. The library keeps it as a record of his tour and its themes.
practical-suggestions-for-mother-and-hou:
Marion Mills Miller wrote Practical Suggestions for Mother and Housewife, edited by Theodore Waters, and the contents reveal a book far more ambitious than its title. Chapter one addresses the single woman and her freedom, arguing culture as a guide to choosing work: daughters as assistants of their fathers. Women in law, in medicine, as scientific farmers, and on the steps of a journalist's career from editor to advertising writer to illustrator of book covers.

Chapter two widens the working map: teaching, book-reviewing, manuscript-reading for publishers, library work, music, painting, and the unmarried daughter at home. Only then do the wife and the house get their chapters, covering marriage's mutual aid, the choice of a home, and supervising a building. Miller wrote professional housework into the same ledger as the professions. The book documents the moment domestic advice grew into vocational guidance for women.
recalled-to-life:
Grant Allen wrote this mystery novel in twenty-one chapters, told by a woman named Una Callingham. Her first recollection opens the tale, and she must begin life again with a past she cannot recall. Photographs carry clues: one chapter gives their story, and another brings yet another photograph.

Una travels from the Grange at Woodbury to Torquay and then to Canada, meeting Dr. Ivor of Babbicombe on the way. Visions of dead years return, suspicions grow hateful, and a strange recognition shakes her plans. The closing titles promise that murder will out, name the real murderer, and let the plot unravel itself.
round-the-red-lamp-being-facts-and-fanci:
Sir Arthur Conan Doyle gathered Round the Red Lamp as facts and fancies of medical life, and he framed the preface as part of a long letter to a friend in America. That friend had warned that sick readers, or women in weak health, would get no good from tales that treat medical life with some truth. Doyle answers that a doctor made more than a puppet needs the darker side shown. Surgeons and doctors, he says, chiefly see that side.

Doyle grants that medical life also shows fine things: courage, heroism, love, and self-giving. Yet those traits, he argues, are called forth by bitter sorrow and trial, so one cannot write of this life and be merry over it. Fiction, in his view, may treat painful things as well as cheerful ones.
rudolph-eucken-a-philosophy-of-life: Abel J. Jones wrote Rudolf Eucken, A Philosophy of Life, issued in London by T. C. and E. C. Jack and in New York by Dodge Publishing. Jones is named as holding degrees from Cambridge and Cardiff posts, and as a former member of the University of Jena. The contents list nine chapters, opening with The Problem of Life, Has the Problem Been Solved, and Another Search for Truth.
scenes-of-clerical-life:
George Eliot wrote Scenes of Clerical Life, presented here in an Everyman's Library printing from Dent in London, first issued in that series in 1910. Three tales make up the collection. The opening tale follows the Rev. Amos Barton and his misfortunes. A second centers on Mr. Gilfil, and a third turns to Janet and her change of heart.

The Barton tale opens with a long look at Shepperton Church as it stood a generation earlier. Only the stone tower and its clock keep their old, familiar face. Around them the building has gained a broad roof, taller windows, polished doors, and clean, smooth walls. Benches, galleries, and an organ complete the picture of a parish church refitted for its congregation.
septimius-felton-or-the-elixir-of-life:
Nathaniel Hawthorne left this romance unfinished at his death, and it reached print in 1871 after his widow began the hard task of reading his late hand. Their daughters finished the copying. An opening note in the 1883 printing tells that story of rescue from loose sheets.

Hawthorne had conceived the tale before The Marble Faun, sparked by a Lancashire legend of a bloody foot that left its print where it passed. A young man seeks a drink said to grant endless life. The note shows how a tale of dark longing survived only through the labor of those who loved its maker.
shandygaff-a-number-of-most-agreeable-in:
Christopher Morley published this gathering of essays, tales, and skits in 1918. Morley jokes that he first wished to name the pieces for a washroom sign in the British Museum. George Gissing, homeless in London, had prized that room's basins until trustees barred full baths there, he recalls.

Morley warns readers that these casual pieces are small cups, not epics. A long section on titles and dedications shows his playful mind at work. Life and letters both come under his gentle probes. The book charms as a young writer's miscellany, half talk, half tale, all in Morley's warm and bookish voice.
short-stories-and-essays-from-literature:
William Dean Howells published this gathering of tales and essays under the head Literature and Life. Contents range from Worries of a Winter Walk and Summer Isles of Eden to A Circus in the Suburbs and At a Dime Museum. American scenes, high and low, fill the list.

The opening walk crosses a cold East River morning in a tenement quarter, where a scrap of motley city life sets Howells pondering. Later pieces treat plagiarism, Puritanism in fiction, and the art of the advertiser. Howells watches modern America with a kind, exact eye, in prose that made him the dean of his country's letters.
some-anomalies-of-the-short-story-from-l:
William Dean Howells takes up odd points about the short story in Some Anomalies of the Short Story, from Literature and Life. A great publishing house, he notes, has begun to bring out sets of short tales one by one. The house hopes that bold persistence will beat the public coldness toward such sets when each book stands alone. Howells says he may pose the puzzles and leave readers to solve them, or to sit puzzled.

His first puzzle is a sharp one. A short tale alone pleases near every reader, yet a book of tales is said to fail. He tests the case of nice folk who lose charm when they share a boarding-house, and finds it wanting. In a magazine, tales sit side by side and shine all the more, and an editor counts his number bright in proportion to the tale writers at his board.
spanish-prisoners-of-war-from-literature:
William Dean Howells recalls a visit to beaten foes in Spanish Prisoners of War. The piece comes from Literature and Life. Some summers back, two cruisers reached Portsmouth, New Hampshire. The St. Louis and the Harvard held Spanish prisoners from Santiago de Cuba. Their count ran to sixteen or seventeen hundred men. Most were sailors and marines from Cervera's fleet. Some were land troops taken before the city.

Howells owns little stomach for war. Yet the fact drew him on its verse-like side. He let the St. Louis sail to Annapolis with Cervera. Then he crossed to Kittery Point and took a boat out. The Harvard lay sullen in the swift Piscataqua. Her paint was a dismal lead color. Her decks were washed, her guns fore and aft. She looked tired and bored. Her work was done, and the living captives lay on an island up the river.
staccato-notes-of-a-vanished-summer-from:
William Dean Howells writes a summer journal in short bursts in Staccato Notes of a Vanished Summer, from Literature and Life. On a Monday afternoon, a storm that had beaten against a southeast wind all day thickens in the northwest. The gale blackens the harbor and whitens the open sea, and sail after sail rounds Whaleback Light and runs for safe anchorage within.

Cautious coasters drop in with a casual air, coal schooners nod to each other on the swell, and small yachts huddle in safe waters. The last craft in before nightfall are mackerel seiners from Gloucester, all of one graceful shape, with seines piled in black heaps. By dark, sixty or seventy ships lie in the harbor. Their lights make a little Venice under the hill, twinkling like the lamps in the basin of St. Mark, between the Maine and New Hampshire coasts.
strife:
John Galsworthy's Strife, a drama in three acts dated 1909, sets the chairman of the Trenartha Tin Plate Works against his own striking workmen. A modern publisher's note at the front traces Galsworthy's career from his first stories in 1897, published under the name John Sinjohn, to fame as a playwright of social questions.

The play's persons begin with John Anthony, the works chairman, an old man of iron will. On the other side stand the men's leaders, worn down by a long strike yet just as stubborn. Galsworthy builds the clash as a duel of two unyielding men, with hunger and pride pressing both camps, and the cost of the deadlock falling on wives and families between them.
study-of-child-life:
Marion Foster Washburne's Study of Child Life forms one volume of The Library of Home Economics, a twelve-volume home-study course issued by the American School of Home Economics at Chicago in 1907. The course bills itself as a complete training in the new profession of home-making and the art of right living.

Teachers of recognized authority prepared the set. They wrote for home-makers, mothers, and teachers. They wrote for physicians, nurses, dietitians, and house managers too. The volumes hold nearly three thousand pages. They hold a thousand illustrations. The course was tested in correspondence instruction. Washburne's volume takes up the child: care, health, training, and growth in the home, treated as a subject worth study rather than guesswork.
such-is-life: Only the front pages of an old electronic text are present here. They carry the standard welcome, copyright cautions, and donation appeals of that early free-text project, and a header line naming the work Such is Life, by Tom Collins and Joseph Furphy. No title page, contents, or chapter text of the novel itself appears in these pages.
tacitus-histories-fyfe:
Tacitus covered Rome's year of civil war, 69 AD, in his Histories. Translator Hamilton Fyfe rendered the surviving books into English. Four emperors rose and fell in that single brutal year.

Armies march, cities burn, and the Capitol itself catches fire. Tacitus writes of Galba, Otho, Vitellius, and Vespasian in turn. Only part of the work survives, ending mid-story. What remains is swift, grim, and superbly told. Read after the Annals, it shows the same pen at work on open war instead of court rot, with equal skill. Fyfe keeps the pace hard and swift.
tales-and-novels-volume-05-tales-of-a-fa:
Volume V of Maria Edgeworth's Tales and Novels holds three Tales of a Fashionable Life: Manoeuvring, Almeria, and Vivian. The ten-volume set, with engravings on steel, collects her adult fiction, and this volume turns on the marriage market of the rich.

The contents give Manoeuvring a long run of numbered chapters before Almeria and Vivian begin. Edgeworth's fashionable world runs on manoeuvre: mothers scheming, fortunes hunted, reputations traded, and young women priced like stock. Against it she sets sense, candor, and the slow education of feeling. Vivian, the third tale, follows a young man of weak resolution through the hands of flatterers and projectors, one of her most searching studies of a character ruined by wanting to please.
the-allis-family-or-scenes-of-western-li:
Issued by the American Sunday-School Union, with its copyright entered in 1858, this short book for young readers follows Mr. and Mrs. Allis on a broad western prairie. No author is named on the pages shown. The family lives far from settled towns while Mr. Allis works at building a farm from raw grassland.

Early pages pause to teach child readers what a prairie is: flat or rolling grass, few trees, no fences in sight. They also explain farm making, from first ploughing with a breaking team onward. Plain lessons about western work sit inside a simple family story meant for Sunday-school shelves.
the-american-frugal-housewife: Title pages and meat-cut plates open The American Frugal Housewife by Mrs. Child, dated 1832 and dedicated to those who are not ashamed of economy. Child is named as author of Hobomok and The Mother's Book and editor of the Juvenile Miscellany. Two mottos praise thrift, one credited to Franklin. The plates label cuts of mutton, pork, and veal piece by piece, from leg and loin to knuckle and breast.
the-battle-of-life:
Charles Dickens set his tale, printed in a Chapman and Hall Christmas Books volume in 1867 and 1868, on an old English battlefield. Part one describes a fierce fight on a long summer day, when grass held blood, streams ran red, and insects were stained by dying men.

Years pass in the telling. Nature recovers, larks sing, crops are sown and gathered, and the stream that ran red turns a watermill. Men whistle at the plough while old people live and die in the town below. Dickens uses that healed ground to frame a later human struggle, fought in daily life rather than with swords.
the-breath-of-life: John Burroughs wrote The Breath of Life, put out in Boston and New York by Houghton Mifflin Company, with rights dated 1915 and a May 1915 release. The chapters start with the title essay, then The Living Wave and A Wonderful World. The Baffling Problem and Scientific Vitalism come next. A Bird of Passage, Life and Mind, and Life and Science fill the mid list. The Journeying Atoms and The Vital Order close the book. Only the title pages and this list are shown, with no essay text.
the-church-and-modern-life:
Washington Gladden wrote this study of the church, dated 1908, in nine chapters that run from the roots of religion to the new leadership. Chapter I limits the field at once. The church under study is the Christian church in the United States, meaning all bodies of Christian disciples organized for work and worship.

That church, Gladden notes, is not one body but many sects and denominations, some with little fellowship among them. A few claim that their own body alone is the true church, and he names the Roman Catholic church and the High Church Episcopalians. Others use the word broadly for all who profess the Christian name. Later chapters ask whether the church is decadent, and treat its business, a coming reformation, social redemption, and a new evangelism. The book argues that faith must answer modern social life directly.
the-colour-of-life:
A set of essays transcribed from the 1897 John Lane edition opens with a title piece on the colour of life. The contents range widely: cloud, winds of the world, the honours of mortality, monastery gates, rushes and reeds, and an essay on Eleonora Duse.

The first essay disputes a common praise. Red is often praised as the noble colour of life. The writer denies the claim: life's true colour, she argues, is not red. Red is the colour of violence, of life broken open, edited, and published. If red is life's colour at all, it is so only when unseen. Fully visible, red becomes the colour of life violated, betrayed, and wasted. The true colour is the covered red of the living heart and pulses, the modest colour of unpublished blood. Such paradox drives these essays, which prize the hidden and implicit over show.
the-crown-of-life:
George Gissing opens The Crown of Life amid the morning rush at Waterloo Station in May of the year '86. A slim, dark, absent-looking young man of twenty-one, Piers Otway, comes out with the suburban crowd. His silk hat and morning coat would pass in the City, but his face would not, and the scramble for omnibus seats leaves him cold.

He crosses the foot-bridge to Charing Cross and drifts into the Haymarket, where a picture shop stops him. Among the engravings, fine landscapes go unnoticed; His eye is caught by the faces and forms of beautiful women. Among them are a great lady in rich dress, a maiden of Hellas on a marble seat, and a sun-browned peasant girl. He cannot tear himself away, and walks on with troubled blood, dreaming of his fate as always at such windows.
the-days-of-my-life: Sir H. Rider Haggard's The Days of My Life, dated 1926 and edited by C. J. Longman, bills itself on the title page as an autobiography. The contents of volume 1 run from childhood and youth through Natal, the special commission to the Transvaal, the annexation, life in the Transvaal, and marriage. Then come a return to England and a chapter named for King Solomon's Mines and She. Only the title pages and that contents list are present here, so the memoir itself does not appear.
the-edge-of-the-knife:
H. Beam Piper's tale The Edge of the Knife ran in Amazing Stories in May 1957. A front note says two top editors turned it down as too hot to handle, and asks readers to judge for themselves. In class, Professor Chalmers states that Khalid ib'n Hussein was shot at Basra in 1973, by an Egyptian with an old U.S. Army gun, and stoned by the crowd.

His students stare: the event has not yet happened. Chalmers recalls past lives and sees what comes. Piper's tale asks how a man who knows the future can prove it, or stay sane.
the-freedom-of-life:
Annie Payson Call wrote The Freedom of Life as a guide to calm, free living, opening with a hymn that asks God to lead his people out of bondage. The contents start with sleep.

Call, author of Power Through Repose, taught that strain and fret waste the body's force. Her chapters take up how to sleep with rest, how to drop worry, and how to meet work and folk without tight nerves. The hymn at the front prays for eyes opened to past bondage and hearts bound to a law of love. Her aim is a daily life ruled by ease rather than fear.
the-greek-view-of-life:
G. Lowes Dickinson wrote The Greek View of Life. Dickinson held the degree M.A. This is the sixth edition, printed at New York in 1909. His preface states the book's purpose. It is a general introduction to Greek literature and thought. It is meant in the first place for those who do not know Greek. Only through translations, he says, can most modern readers reach Greek culture. 

Dickinson owns that his title begs a question. Yet he believes it has a clear meaning. The phases of Greek civilization are varied. Still, they group themselves about certain main ideas. Those ideas can be told apart from the ideas that ruled other nations. He has tried to bring those main ideas into relief. He avoids matter of dispute as far as he can. He asks scholars to judge it by its fitness for its end.
the-heir-of-redclyffe: Charlotte M. Yonge wrote The Heir of Redclyffe, with a heading in the record dated 1853. The contents list chapters numbered 1 through 19, with no titles given for any of them. Only the title page and contents list are present here, so the novel itself does not appear. A second record in the library carries the same title and author, and that record opens with the first chapter itself.
the-house-of-life:
Dante Gabriel Rossetti gathered his sonnets under this title. Part I carries the heading Youth and Change. The first sonnet defines the form itself. A sonnet is a moment's monument. It is a memorial carved in ivory or ebony. It is also a coin. Its face reveals the soul. Its reverse shows the power the soul serves.

The next sonnet is Love Enthroned. Love sits above Truth, Hope, Fame, Youth, and Life. His throne stands in breathless bowers. The kindred powers cannot dream of that place. Bridal Birth follows in the sequence. Readers who continue get a long meditation on love, time, and death. Rossetti builds it one strict fourteen-line room at a time.
the-lights-and-shadows-of-real-life:
T. S. Arthur published his sketches of life and character at Philadelphia in 1851, and his preface frames the title in moral weather. Light and shadow come to everyone, he says, yet clouds in a life rise from below, from evil in the mind, not from a pure heaven.

Trials can clear that sky as better purposes grow through pain. A publisher introduction adds a short autobiography of Arthur as a self made man who rose through patient labor against adverse pressure. His temperance tales and domestic stories aimed to push readers toward reform at home.
the-lion-and-the-mouse-a-story-of-americ: Charles Klein wrote the play behind this novel, and Arthur Hornblow novelized it for Grosset and Dunlap in August 1906. Only the front pages and the start of a bare contents list are present here, showing a frontispiece of Shirley appealing to Mr. Ryder to go to Washington and save her father life. A Pope couplet warns that judges and senators have been bought for gold. The novel itself cannot be read in this record.
the-lion-and-the-mouse-a-story-of-an-ame: Charles Klein wrote the play behind this novel, and Arthur Hornblow novelized it as a story of an American life. Only the title page and a bare contents list of fifteen chapters are present here, with no story text at all. Its Pope epigraph reads slightly differently from the companion record of this title, giving Senates where the other gives Senators. The tale of a senator daughter facing down a railroad magnate is absent from this record.
the-lord-of-death-and-the-queen-of-life:
Homer Eon Flint's The Lord of Death and the Queen of Life opens Part I, The Discovery, inside a remarkable car. Four men ride in it: a doctor who sings a cheerful baritone, a geologist peeling potatoes, an architect named Jackson, and Smith, the engineer, who tends machinery with an oil-can. Their car draws an anti-gravitation current through tunnels, and Jackson demands to know how Smith pulls electricity from the ether without blasting them all to cinders.

Smith answers that the air around the earth is full of electricity. He looks unimportant, mild, and good-humored, yet his skull holds an unusually complete knowledge of electricity and mechanisms. Flint starts his science-fiction tale as a working trip among friends, with the wonder explained over song and potatoes.
the-mayor-s-wife:
Anna Katherine Green's novel The Mayor's Wife opens with a young woman badly in need of a position. She watches Miss Davies, who runs an employment office, enter with the air of someone carrying an unusually fine offer. The narrator admits she cannot hide all traces of her anxiety. Others in the room need work less desperately than she does.

The contents map the mystery she walks into: strange neighbors next door, a moving shadow, and scraps of evidence. Later chapters promise a cipher, a wife's tale, the sins of the fathers, and a finger on the wall. Titles such as In the Gable Window and The Cry from the Stairs keep the suspense domestic and close. Green, a pioneer of detective fiction, builds her puzzle inside a mayor's household, where a hired companion watches everything.
the-nervous-housewife:
Abraham Myerson's The Nervous Housewife was published in Boston by Little, Brown and Company in November 1920. Its contents map a study in thirteen chapters. They cover the nature of nervousness and the types of housewife predisposed to it. Housework and the home appear as factors in the neurosis, and poverty's effects on the mind get a chapter. Later chapters treat the housewife and her husband, symptoms used as weapons against the husband, case histories, treatment, and the future of woman, the home, and marriage.

Chapter I opens by asking how long the problem of the nervous housewife has existed. Myerson wonders, half in jest, whether the cave man's wife wept over her house-cleaning or complained of her back when he returned from a prehistoric hunt. The problem, the opening implies, may be as old as the home itself.
